newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Rafsanjani to visit Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Rafsanjani to visit Turkey.

text.p: Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani visits neighbouring Turkey on Thursday to strengthen ties despite U.S. efforts to isolate Iran.
The visit, which is at the invitation of Turkish President Suleyman Demirel, is significant in terms of economic, political and regional cooperation, Iranian newspapers said.
"We are genuinely collaborating with Turkey. We are Moslem neighbours and as neighbours we have long cooperated with each other," Rafsanjani said on the eve of the visit.
He said in an interview there were projects that ensured economic profit to both countries and thus brought them closer together, and a spirit of collaboration prevailed.
Excerpts from the interview with Turkish television and the Ankara Daily News on Tuesday were released by the Iranian state news agency IRNA.
The Tehran Times said on Wednesday the visit indicated that both countries planned to further upgrade their relations.

"As two Moslem countries, Iran and Turkey have many reasons for upgrading mutual cooperation. Both possess sufficient skilled manpower, a high productivity in agriculture, both are situated in a strategic part of the world, and are members of many regional organisations; both share borders with the newly independent republics of the former Soviet Union, and the two nations have a long period of friendship."

Irano-Turkish relations were boosted in August when Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, visited Iran where he signed a $23 billion agreement for the supply of Iranian natural gas over 23 years.
The deal was struck days after U.S. President Bill Clinton signed a law imposing sanctions on any country investing more than $40 million a year in the energy industries of Iran and Libya.
The Clinton administration accuses Iran and Libya of sponsoring international terrorism and pursues a "dual containment" policy aimed at isolating Iran and Iraq.
The Turkish government said the deal would not be affected by U.S. sanctions because Turkey would construct a 300 km (190 mile) gas pipeline on its own soil from Tabriz to Ankara.
Not all Iranians hail the trend of warmer relations. Some still see Turkey, a key NATO member and base for U.S. warplanes, as an extension of U.S. influence in a mostly Moslem region.

Jomhuri Eslami daily urged caution in expanding relations with Ankara and said nothing would change as long as the backbone of U.S. military and security was preserved in the joint Turkish-U.S. air base at Incirlik in southern Turkey.
Iran, like much of the Moslem world, was angered earlier this year when Turkey signed a deal with Israel, allowing Israeli airforce planes to train in Turkish airspace.
Earlier this month Turkey renewed a military cooperation pact with Israel which provided for exercises in 1997.
